Disavow

/dis-uh-VOW/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Disavow means to deny knowledge of, responsibility for, or association with something.

The candidate moved quickly to disavow the insulting flyer, insisting that no one on her staff had approved it.

Worked Example

When a wellness blog claimed his sleep study proved that naps cure illness, Dr. Ferro published a letter to disavow the claim. He explained that his research had never tested anything of the kind, and he wanted no association with the exaggeration.

Dr. Ferro publicly denies any connection between himself and the blog's claim, which is exactly what it means to disavow something.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disclaim: To disclaim is to state formally that you have no claim to or responsibility for something - companies disclaim liability in fine print. Disavow is more personal and pointed: a public figure disavows a statement or an ally to cut off any association with it. Disclaiming manages legal exposure; disavowing defends a reputation.

renounce: To renounce is to formally give up something you actually held - a title, a claim, a belief you once professed. To disavow is to deny that a connection exists at all, or to reject responsibility for it. You renounce what was yours; you disavow what you insist was never yours.

reject: To reject is simply to refuse to accept something - an offer, an idea, an application - and it can be entirely private. To disavow is a public, on-the-record act: openly denying any association with the thing. You can reject a plan silently in your head; disavowing it requires an audience.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

acknowledge: to admit or accept as true

endorse: to publicly support or approve

Where it sits · how strong and public the refusal is — deny → disavow → repudiate

deny vs. disavow: To deny is the everyday act of saying something is not true, while to disavow is a more formal, public refusal to be connected with it.

repudiate vs. disavow: To disavow is to deny any association, but to repudiate is even stronger, a complete and often dramatic rejection of the thing itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: not, opposite of

Root — avow

Root — avow: to declare or affirm openly

Put it together

Put it together: Disavow pairs dis-, meaning not or opposite of, with avow, to declare or affirm openly, which traces back to the Latin votum, a vow. To disavow is literally to un-declare something, taking back any claim of connection.

Use the root in a new word: avow

Use the root in a new word: avow: The mayor stood before the crowd to avow her commitment to finishing the park project.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / public statements

Disavow almost always describes a public, on-the-record denial, often by an official, an organization, or a public figure. If you privately doubt something, you are merely skeptical; when you formally announce you have no part in it, you disavow it.
